source: McKinsey Quarterly (2006) Improving strategic planning: A McKinsey Survey
finding: Online survey of executives. Most firms have a formal planning process, but few say it drives their most important decisions. Fewer than half are satisfied with how their firm makes strategy.
numbers: N=796 responses, late July to early August 2006, worldwide panel, financial or strategy roles, firms with revenue of at least $500M, data weighted by GDP. Over 75% have a formal process; fewer than 25% say the process is key to their most important decisions. Exhibit 1: 52% say a small senior group including the CEO decides, 23% decide with the formal planning process, 11% business-unit leaders, 10% CEO alone. Among firms with a process: 14% extremely significant, 44% very, 29% somewhat, 10% slightly, 3% not at all. 79% of satisfied respondents say the process plays a significant role.
quote: fewer than a quarter say that the process is key to making their most important decisions
limits: Self-report, one wave, large firms only, no performance outcome. Satisfaction and process use are correlated within the same respondents. The Wikipedia line about key decisions rests on this survey (gap 8 closed).
agent_relevance: Having a plan and using it for the big decision are different. Our agent should make the option-generation step bind the final choice, not sit beside it.

source: Boyd (1991) Strategic planning and financial performance: a meta-analytic review (J Management Studies)
finding: Pooled 29 samples. Found modest correlations between planning and nine performance measures. Author says measurement problems likely make this understate the true link.
numbers: 29 samples, 2,496 organisations. Pooled r, CI and I2 not obtainable: Wiley and Semantic Scholar full text blocked; abstract came via Crossref text only.
limits: Abstract level only. Old, mostly small-firm samples.
agent_relevance: Effect is real but small in the oldest meta-analysis. Do not expect large gains from a plan step alone.

source: George, Walker and Monster (2019) Does strategic planning improve organizational performance? A meta-analysis (Public Administration Review)
finding: Random-effects meta-analysis finds a positive, moderate, significant effect of strategic planning on organisational performance. Strongest when performance is effectiveness and planning is formal. Holds in public and private sectors, US and non-US.
numbers: 87 correlations from 31 studies. Pooled r, CI, I2 and bias tests not read (full text 403).
limits: Public administration journal, so earlier labelling as a business meta-analysis needs care. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Supports plan-step value but not its size. Formal planning beats informal.

source: Hamann, Halw and Guenther (2022) Meta-analysis of the corporate planning-organizational performance relationship: a research note (Strategic Management Journal)
finding: 183 independent samples, 84 new versus earlier reviews. Corrects for measurement error and dichotomisation. Effect stable over time and across planning types. Larger for manufacturing, larger firms, high uncertainty avoidance countries and high environmental uncertainty. Depends on how planning and performance are measured.
numbers: k=183 samples. Pooled corrected r, CI, I2 and publication-bias results not read (Wiley 403 on html, pdf and xml; only Crossref summaries).
limits: Management summary: planning is definitely correlated with performance, but effects are conditional on measurement type. Gap 1 stays open for the number.
agent_relevance: Planning helps more when uncertainty is high. Consistent with a difficulty-scaled planning budget, but firms are not LLM agents.

source: Delmar and Shane (2003) Does business planning facilitate the development of new ventures? (Strategic Management Journal)
finding: Business planning lowers the chance a new venture is disbanded and speeds product development and venture organising. Authors present planning as a precursor to action.
numbers: 223 new ventures started in the first 9 months of 1998, random sample of Swedish founders. Effect sizes not obtained.
limits: Abstract via Crossref only. One country, one cohort, observational; selection into planning not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Planning as precursor to action fits a plan-then-act scaffold.

source: Brinckmann, Grichnik and Kapsa (2010) Should entrepreneurs plan or just storm the castle? (J Business Venturing)
finding: Meta-analysis of contextual factors in the planning-performance link for small firms. Cited 769 times per Semantic Scholar. Publisher withholds abstract.
numbers: No numbers obtained. Publisher blocks abstract and PDF.
limits: Gap 9 only half closed: title and scope confirmed, effect sizes and moderators not read.
agent_relevance: None yet.

source: Fredrickson and Mitchell (1984) Strategic decision processes: comprehensiveness and performance in an industry with an unstable environment; Dean and Sharfman (1996) Does decision process matter?
finding: Retrieval failed. Both are JSTOR papers and Crossref holds no abstract. The only related record found is Dean and Sharfman (1993): 61 strategic decisions in 24 companies, procedural rationality and political behaviour were independent dimensions.
numbers: No comprehensiveness-performance coefficients obtained for either paper.
limits: Gap 2 remains open. Remembered effect sizes are not recorded as read.
agent_relevance: K17 stays single-source.

source: Girotra, Meincke, Terwiesch and Ulrich (2023) Ideas are dimes a dozen: LLMs for idea generation in innovation (Wharton working paper)
finding: GPT-4 generated product ideas for college students faster and cheaper than students, with higher average purchase intent and higher variance. Most of the best ideas came from GPT-4.
numbers: 400 ideas rated on mTurk (200 student, 100 GPT-4 plain, 100 GPT-4 seeded with good examples), about 20 ratings each. Mean purchase intent: students 40.4%, GPT-4 46.8%, GPT-4 with examples 49.3% (human vs GPT p<0.001; two GPT arms p=0.11). Top decile (40 ideas): 35 (87.5%) from GPT-4. Best idea 11% higher purchase probability than best human idea. Speed: about 800 ideas/hour vs about 20 for a human alone; cost about $0.63 per idea at $500/hour, API fee about $20 for 800 ideas. Novelty: humans higher (p<0.001); novelty vs purchase intent r=-0.08 (p=0.12).
quote: ChatGPT-4 can generate ideas much faster and cheaper than students
limits: GPT-4-0314, temperature 0.7, one domain (cheap student products); consumer survey as quality proxy, not market outcomes. No expert-ranking correlation. Not strategy decisions.
agent_relevance: Quantity plus selection works for generation when quality can be rated. The rating step is the cost: here a human survey, not a model.

source: Meincke, Mollick and Terwiesch (2024) Prompting diverse ideas: increasing AI idea variance
finding: Plain GPT-4 idea pools are less diverse than human group pools. Chain-of-thought brainstorming gets close to human diversity. Measures diversity, not idea quality.
numbers: Cosine similarity: human group pool 0.243 vs GPT-4 0.255 to 0.432 across prompts; baseline 0.377, Steve Jobs persona 0.368, HBR creativity tools 0.387. 35 prompts compared; 100 ideas per session, 10 sessions per prompt. Unique ideas in the domain about 3,700 (base) to 4,700 (CoT).
limits: Diversity only. No link to final decision quality. Single product domain. GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: A plan or CoT step before listing options widens the option pool. Whether wider pools give better final choices is not tested here.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning in natural language improves LLM search for code generation (PlanSearch)
finding: Generating many diverse natural-language plans before code raises best-of-k performance. LLM-judged idea diversity strongly predicts how much search helps. Pass@1 sometimes falls because diversity dilutes the best idea.
numbers: LiveCodeBench pass@200 repeated sampling vs PlanSearch: GPT-4o-mini 53.3 vs 64.9; GPT-4o 60.6 vs 73.0; DeepSeek-Coder-V2 53.2 vs 70.3; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 55.6 vs 77.0 (its pass@1 is 40.3). With public-test filtering PlanSearch reaches 77.1% at pass@20 vs 77.0% at pass@200 without filtering. With public-test filtering PlanSearch is ahead by a flat 30 to 40 points at 10 completions. HumanEval+ Claude 88.9 to 98.5; MBPP+ 83.0 to 93.7. o1-mini: 90.8 repeated vs 91.3 PlanSearch (gap small). Main plots are equal attempts; Appendix D gives compute-normalised plots and the authors say findings are highly similar.
quote: diversity score accounts for much of the variance
limits: Code has a test checker, so selection is reliable. Diversity-gain relation shown as a scatter (Figure 6), no coefficient located in text. Does not cover open-ended strategy.
agent_relevance: Closest answer to gap 3: more distinct plans before acting helps, at roughly matched compute, but only with a checker. Track idea diversity, not only count.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu and Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Allocating by difficulty beat best-of-N with about 4x less compute. On easy questions extra search hurts; on hard questions search helps; on the hardest almost nothing helps.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S*. Five difficulty bins from the model's own pass rate (2048 samples per problem). About 4x less compute than best-of-N for revisions and for PRM search. FLOPs-matched against a 14x larger model: test-time compute preferable on easy and medium questions, not on the hardest. Beam search degrades on levels 1 and 2 as budget grows, beats best-of-N on levels 3 and 4, no method progresses on level 5. Model-predicted difficulty costs extra compute versus oracle difficulty.
limits: Math with a learned verifier, one model family, 2024. Not planning for open-ended judgment.
agent_relevance: Direct support for gap 6: a difficulty-scaled budget works for LLMs, and over-optimising against a weak verifier hurts on easy items.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo and Griffiths (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Explicit reasoning can lower accuracy. In three of six tasks taken from human psychology, large drops with chain-of-thought; in others mixed. In a many-feature choice task (apartments), reasoning mostly helped.
numbers: Artificial grammar learning: o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o zero-shot 94.0% on a 440-problem subset (36.3 point drop); GPT-4o 87.5% vs 64.4% with CoT (-23.1, p<0.0001); Claude 3 Opus 70.7 vs 62.7; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 vs 67.7 (no drop). Apartment choice: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 81% to 95% with CoT in the top weight range; Llama 3.1 70B fell (43% to 20%) because it often gave no answer. Bootstrap over 378 comparisons supports the human-to-model heuristic.
limits: 2024 models (o1-preview, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5). CoT is not plan-first, but it is the nearest evidence on judgment-type tasks. No equal-token control for o1-preview.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly answered: on non-math judgment tasks more reasoning can hurt, so a plan step must be tested, not assumed.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute (TMLR)
finding: Tasks exist where longer reasoning lowers accuracy in frontier reasoning models. Five failure modes: Claude distracted by irrelevant data, o-series overfit to problem framing, drift to spurious correlations, loss of focus on constraint tasks, stronger self-preservation language in Claude Sonnet 4.
numbers: Four task groups: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction with constraint tracking, advanced AI risk. Requested reasoning budgets 0 to 16,384 tokens; actual tokens up to about 20k. Few-shot examples largely fixed the regression failure. Abstract, introduction and setup read; per-model accuracy tables not extracted.
limits: Synthetic tasks built to elicit the effect. Shows existence, not how often it happens in real work.
agent_relevance: More thinking is not safe by default for 2025 models. Cap reasoning length and test for it.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do not think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend large token budgets on trivial questions, and later solution rounds add little. A self-training method cuts tokens without losing accuracy.
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1 on GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME, ASDIV. Most instances (76 to 80% for QwQ, 59 to 63% for R1) give 2 to 4 solution rounds. Exact savings figures not extracted this session.
limits: Efficiency, not accuracy loss. Math-heavy.
agent_relevance: Supports difficulty-scaled thinking: spend little on easy items.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: Strong LLM judges (GPT-4) agree with human preferences over 80% of the time, the same level as human-human agreement. Judges show position bias, verbosity bias and self-enhancement bias, and weak reasoning on math.
numbers: Agreement above 80% with humans on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. Most judges favour the first position in swapped-order tests.
limits: Chat-quality preferences, not strategy outcomes. Agreement with humans is not agreement with ground truth.
agent_relevance: A model judge is a usable but biased verifier substitute for gap 7. Swap order and use several judges.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park and Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd
finding: An ensemble of 12 LLMs forecasts about as accurately as a 925-person human crowd on 31 binary questions. Acquiescence bias above 50% seen.
numbers: LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12), human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850; no-information benchmark 0.25. Single models in Table 2 range from GPT-4 0.15 to Mistral-7B 0.24. Study 2: showing the human median to GPT-4 or Claude 2 improved accuracy by 17 to 28%; averaging human and machine forecasts was better.
limits: 31 questions, one three-month tournament, 2024 models. Ground truth comes later, so it is not a live verifier.
agent_relevance: Aggregating many independent samples is the verifier-free substitute with measured results. Same logic as Doshi 2024.

source: Doshi, Bell, Mirzayev and Vanneste (2024) Generative AI and evaluating strategic decisions (SSRN / Strategic Management Journal)
finding: Two studies of 60 business models each (AI-generated and competition entries) compare LLM rankings with human experts. Single AI evaluations are inconsistent and biased. Aggregated across models, roles and prompts, they resemble expert rankings.
numbers: Two studies, 60 business models each. Correlations with expert rankings, bias sizes and cost not obtained: SSRN 403 and Wiley 403.
limits: Abstract via Crossref only. Gap 4 half closed (Girotra read in full, Doshi not).
agent_relevance: Judging strategic options with one LLM call is unreliable. Average many calls with varied roles.

source: Camuffo, Cordova, Gambardella and Spina (2020) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making: evidence from a randomized control trial (Management Science)
finding: 116 Italian startups, about one year, 10 sessions each. Treated firms learned to build theories and run falsifiable tests. They performed better, pivoted more and did not drop out more than control in the early stages.
numbers: 116 startups, 16 data points. Registry: 59 treatment, 57 control, 21 mentors, same hours in both arms; power 0.61 for |rho|=0.1, 0.94 for 0.3.
limits: Abstract level. Treatment is hypothesis testing, not planning. Control was intuition plus generic customer-feedback training.
agent_relevance: Option: a hypothesis-testing step with decision thresholds.

source: AEA RCT Registry AEARCTR-0002205 (Camuffo): A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision making (second Italian trial)
finding: Second Bocconi trial run 2017 to 2019. Registry shows no results but says associated papers report treated startups assess ideas more precisely, close more often, pivot toward better ideas and perform better.
numbers: Planned 265 startups (132/133); final 257 clusters or 250 observations (registry gives both); 125 per arm; 8 sessions; seven instructors; primary outcomes revenue, dropout, pivots.
limits: Registry page, not a paper; counts conflict. Result statements are the registry's summary of other papers.
agent_relevance: A replication exists and is described as the same direction.

source: Camuffo, Gambardella, Messinese, Novelli, Paolucci and Spina (2024) A scientific approach to entrepreneurial decision-making: large-scale replication and extension (Strategic Management Journal)
finding: Four randomized trials with 759 firms replicate the 2020 study. Positive effect on idea termination. Radical pivots show a non-linear effect: treated firms make a few pivots, not none or many.
numbers: 759 firms, four RCTs. Revenue effect size not stated in the abstract; headline outcomes are termination and pivots.
limits: Abstract only. The headline outcomes are termination and pivots, so the original 'performs better' claim is not clearly carried over. Same research group.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-testing training is the one planning-like intervention with a randomised replication. Effect shows on stopping bad ideas, less clearly on revenue.

source: AEA RCT Registry AEARCTR-0006578 (Italy trial) and AEARCTR-0015080 (Uruguay replication, Segantini)
finding: Italy 2016 trial (116 startups, 59/57) was registered late, in October 2020. An independent replication in Uruguay is registered for September 2025 to September 2026 with no results yet.
numbers: Uruguay: two experiments, each with at least 116 nascent entrepreneurs (58/58), up to 1,392 observations, four-month programme; outcomes revenue, time to first client, termination, pivots.
limits: Registrations only. Uruguay results not yet available.
agent_relevance: An independent replication will show whether the effect holds outside Italy.
